questions.q: JVM stands for:
options: Java Virtual Machine, which executes Java bytecode

questions.q: Which of the following is responsible for converting Java bytecode into machine-specific instructions at runtime?
JRE stands for:
options: Java Runtime Environment, which provides libraries and JVM needed to run Java applications

questions.q: JDK stands for:
options: Java Development Kit, which includes JRE plus development tools like the compiler

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between JDK, JRE, and JVM?
options: JVM contains JRE, which contains JDK
JDK contains JRE, which contains JVM, along with development tools like javac
JRE contains JDK, which contains JVM
They are unrelated and independent components

questions.q: The component that makes Java 'platform independent' by allowing the same bytecode to run on different operating systems is the:
options: JVM, since each platform has its own JVM implementation that interprets the same bytecode

questions.q: Which tool in the JDK is used to compile .java source files into .class bytecode files?
Java's primitive data types include all of the following EXCEPT:
Implicit type casting (widening conversion) in Java occurs when:
options: A smaller data type is automatically converted to a larger compatible data type, e.g., int to double
A larger data type is automatically converted to a smaller data type without any cast
A String is automatically converted to an int
Casting always requires an explicit cast operator

questions.q: Explicit type casting (narrowing conversion) in Java requires:
options: An explicit cast operator, e.g., (int) someDouble, since it may lead to data loss
The use of the new keyword
The variable to be declared final

questions.q: What is the default value of a boolean instance variable in Java if not explicitly initialized?
What is the size, in bits, of a Java int primitive type?
Which primitive data type in Java is used to store a single 16-bit Unicode character?
Converting a double value to an int in Java by narrowing conversion typically results in:
options: Truncation of the fractional part (decimal digits are discarded)

questions.q: A constructor in Java is:
options: A special method used to initialize objects, having the same name as the class and no return type
A method that must always return an int
A static method used to destroy objects
A keyword used to declare interfaces

questions.q: If a Java class does not define any constructor explicitly, the compiler:
options: Leaves the class without any way to be instantiated
Automatically provides a no-argument default constructor

questions.q: An object in Java is created using which keyword?
Constructor overloading in Java means:
options: A class can have multiple constructors with different parameter lists
A class can have only one constructor
A constructor can be inherited and overridden like a normal method

questions.q: Can a Java constructor have a return type like void?
options: Yes, constructors can return void explicitly
No, constructors have no return type at all, not even void
Yes, but only for abstract classes
Only static constructors can have a return type

questions.q: The 'this' keyword used inside a constructor to call another constructor of the same class is written as:
In Java, a class inherits from another class using the keyword:
In Java, a class implements an interface using the keyword:
Does Java support multiple inheritance of classes (a class extending more than one class directly)?
options: Yes, a Java class can extend multiple classes directly
No, Java does not support multiple inheritance of classes; a class can extend only one class
Yes, but only for abstract classes

questions.q: Does Java support a class implementing multiple interfaces?
options: No, a class can implement only one interface
Yes, a Java class can implement multiple interfaces separated by commas
Only abstract classes can implement multiple interfaces
Interfaces cannot be implemented by classes

questions.q: Every class in Java, unless it explicitly extends another class, implicitly extends:
An interface in Java, prior to Java 8, could only contain:
options: Public abstract methods and public static final variables (constants)

questions.q: Since Java 8, interfaces can also contain:
options: Only abstract methods as before, with no changes
Default and static methods with implementations

questions.q: The 'super' keyword in Java is primarily used to:
options: Refer to the current class instance
Refer to the immediate parent class, to access its members or call its constructor

questions.q: The 'this' keyword in Java is primarily used to:
options: Refer to the current object instance, often to resolve naming conflicts between instance variables and parameters

questions.q: To explicitly call the parent class constructor from a subclass constructor in Java, you use:
If used, a call to super() or this() inside a constructor must be:
options: Placed anywhere in the constructor body
The first statement in the constructor
The last statement in the constructor
Omitted entirely if the class has a constructor

questions.q: Which keyword would you use to access a parent class's method that has been overridden in the subclass?
Can 'this()' and 'super()' both be used as the first statement in the same constructor?
options: Yes, both can appear together as the first two statements
No, only one of this() or super() can be used, and it must be the first statement in the constructor
Neither can ever be used in a constructor
Only this() is allowed in any constructor

questions.q: Method overloading in Java refers to:
options: Defining multiple methods in the same class with the same name but different parameter lists
Redefining a parent class method in a subclass with the same signature
Using the same method name in unrelated classes

questions.q: Method overriding in Java refers to:
options: A subclass providing a new implementation for a method already defined in its superclass, with the same signature
Defining multiple methods with different parameter lists in the same class
Renaming a method in the subclass

questions.q: Method overloading is resolved:
options: At compile time, based on the method signature (compile-time/static polymorphism)
At runtime, based on the actual object type (runtime polymorphism)
By the JVM class loader only

questions.q: Method overriding is resolved:
options: At runtime, based on the actual object type (runtime/dynamic polymorphism)
By the compiler using static binding
It cannot be resolved in Java

questions.q: Which annotation is commonly used in Java to indicate that a method is intended to override a superclass method?
Can static methods be overridden in Java?
options: Yes, static methods can be overridden just like instance methods
No, static methods can be hidden (method hiding) but not truly overridden, since they are resolved at compile time

questions.q: For method overriding to be valid, the overriding method in the subclass must have:
options: A completely different parameter list from the parent method
The same name, same parameter list, and a compatible return type as the parent method
A different name but same parameters

sections.name: Abstract Class vs Interface in Java

questions.q: An abstract class in Java is declared using the keyword:
Can an abstract class in Java have both abstract and concrete (fully implemented) methods?
options: No, it can only have abstract methods
Yes, an abstract class can have a mix of abstract methods and regular implemented methods
No, it can only have concrete methods
Only if it implements an interface

questions.q: Can an abstract class in Java be instantiated directly using new?
options: No, an abstract class cannot be instantiated directly; it must be subclassed
Only if it has a constructor
Only if it has no abstract methods

questions.q: A key difference between an abstract class and an interface in Java (traditionally) is that:
options: An abstract class can have constructors and instance variables with state, while a traditional interface primarily defines a contract
Interfaces can have constructors while abstract classes cannot
Abstract classes cannot have any methods
There is no difference between them

questions.q: Regarding multiple inheritance, a Java class can:
options: Extend multiple abstract classes but implement only one interface
Extend only one abstract class but implement multiple interfaces
Extend multiple abstract classes and implement multiple interfaces
Neither extend multiple classes nor implement multiple interfaces

questions.q: When should you generally prefer an interface over an abstract class in Java design?
options: When you need to define a contract that unrelated classes can implement, without needing to share a common base state
When you need to store significant shared state (instance variables) across a class hierarchy
When you never want the type to be implemented by any class
When you want to prevent polymorphism

questions.q: A member declared as private in a Java class is accessible:
options: Only within the class in which it is declared
Only from subclasses in other packages

questions.q: A member declared as public in a Java class is accessible:
options: From anywhere the class itself is accessible, including other packages

questions.q: A member declared as protected in a Java class is accessible:
options: Only within the exact same class
Within the same package, and also from subclasses in different packages

questions.q: If no access modifier is specified for a member in Java (default/package-private access), it is accessible:
options: Only within classes in the same package
Only within the exact same class
Only from subclasses regardless of package

questions.q: Which access modifier provides the most restrictive access in Java?
Can a top-level Java class be declared as private?
options: Yes, any class can be private
No, a top-level class can only be public or default (package-private), not private or protected
Only abstract classes can be private
Only final classes can be private

sections.name: Exception Handling (try-catch-finally, throw, throws, custom exceptions)

questions.q: In Java, the block of code that might throw an exception is placed inside:
A catch block in Java is used to:
options: Declare that a method might throw an exception
Handle an exception that was thrown in the corresponding try block
Always execute regardless of whether an exception occurred

questions.q: The finally block in a try-catch-finally structure in Java:
options: Executes only if an exception is thrown
Generally executes regardless of whether an exception was thrown or caught, typically used for cleanup
Never executes if the try block completes successfully
Replaces the need for a catch block entirely

questions.q: The 'throw' keyword in Java is used to:
options: Declare that a method might throw a checked exception in its signature
Explicitly throw an instance of an exception from within code

questions.q: The 'throws' keyword in Java is used to:
options: Declare in a method signature that the method might throw one or more checked exceptions
Catch an exception in a catch block

questions.q: A custom exception in Java is typically created by:
options: Extending the Exception class (or a subclass like RuntimeException)
Declaring a static method named exception()
Using the throws keyword alone with no class definition

questions.q: Checked exceptions in Java differ from unchecked exceptions in that:
options: Checked exceptions must be either caught or declared with throws, while unchecked exceptions (like RuntimeException) do not have this requirement
Unchecked exceptions must always be caught at compile time
Checked exceptions are always subclasses of Error
There is no real difference between them

questions.q: A static member in a Java class belongs to:
options: The class itself, shared across all instances of that class

questions.q: A static method in Java can be called:
options: Directly using the class name, without creating an instance
Only if the class is abstract

questions.q: Declaring a variable as final in Java means:
options: Its value can be changed as many times as needed
Its value, once assigned, cannot be changed (it becomes a constant reference or value)
It can only be used inside loops

questions.q: Declaring a method as final in Java means:
options: The method can be overridden freely by subclasses
The method cannot be overridden by any subclass
The method cannot be called at all

questions.q: Declaring a class as final in Java means:
options: The class can be extended by any number of subclasses
The class cannot be subclassed/extended at all
The class must contain only static members

questions.q: A static block in a Java class is primarily used to:
options: Initialize static variables or run setup code once, when the class is first loaded

questions.q: A package in Java is primarily used to:
options: Group related classes and interfaces together and help avoid naming conflicts
Compile Java source code into bytecode

questions.q: Which keyword is used at the top of a Java source file to declare that its classes belong to a specific package?
Which keyword is used in Java to bring classes from another package into the current file for use?
The java.lang package in Java, containing classes like String and Object, is:
options: Never available and must always be manually imported
Automatically imported into every Java program without an explicit import statement
Only available in Java versions before 8
Only usable within the same package

questions.q: If a Java class has no explicit package declaration, it belongs to:
options: No package at all, causing a compile error

questions.q: The directory structure required for Java packages typically:
options: Has no relationship to the package name at all
Mirrors the package name, e.g., classes in package com.example.util reside in a com/example/util directory
Must always be a single flat folder for all classes
Is generated only at runtime by the JVM

questions.q: In Java, a thread can be created by:
options: Extending the Thread class or implementing the Runnable interface
Only by using static methods in the Object class

questions.q: Which method is called to actually start a new thread of execution in Java (rather than running it on the current thread)?
Calling the run() method directly on a Thread object (instead of start()):
options: Starts a new thread of execution as expected
Executes the run() method's code on the current calling thread, without creating a new thread

questions.q: The synchronized keyword in Java is used to:
options: Control access to a block of code or method so that only one thread can execute it at a time on a given object, preventing race conditions

questions.q: A thread in Java can be in which of the following states?
options: New, Runnable, Blocked/Waiting, Timed Waiting, and Terminated, among others

questions.q: The main() method in a standard Java application runs on which thread by default?
options: The main thread, created automatically by the JVM when the program starts
No thread; it runs outside any thread
A thread the programmer must create manually

questions.q: In Java, String objects are:
options: Mutable, meaning their content can be changed after creation
Immutable, meaning once created, their content cannot be changed

questions.q: StringBuilder in Java is primarily used when:
options: You need thread-safe, synchronized string manipulation
You need a mutable sequence of characters that can be modified efficiently, especially in single-threaded contexts
You want to avoid using the String class entirely for constants

questions.q: How does StringBuffer differ from StringBuilder in Java?
options: StringBuffer is immutable while StringBuilder is mutable
StringBuffer is synchronized (thread-safe) while StringBuilder is not synchronized, making StringBuilder generally faster in single-threaded code
They are identical in every respect
StringBuffer cannot be used to build strings at all

questions.q: Concatenating Strings repeatedly using the + operator in a loop is generally discouraged because:
options: Since Strings are immutable, each concatenation can create a new String object, which is inefficient; StringBuilder is preferred for such cases
The + operator does not work with Strings
It automatically converts to StringBuffer, which is always slower

questions.q: Which class would you typically use for building a string through many modifications in a multithreaded environment requiring synchronization?
String literals in Java, such as "hello", are typically stored in:
options: A special memory area called the String pool (part of the heap), enabling reuse of identical literals
Static memory reserved only for primitives
They are not stored anywhere until explicitly assigned

questions.q: Wrapper classes in Java are used to:
options: Represent primitive data types as objects, e.g., Integer for int, Double for double
Replace all classes with static methods

questions.q: The process of automatically converting a primitive type to its corresponding wrapper object in Java is called:
The process of automatically converting a wrapper object back to its corresponding primitive type in Java is called:
Which of the following is the wrapper class for the primitive type int in Java?
Wrapper classes are commonly needed when working with Java Collections (like ArrayList) because:
options: Collections can only store primitive types directly
Collections can only store objects, not primitives, so primitives must be wrapped
Wrapper classes are faster than primitives in all cases
Primitives cannot be declared in Java at all

questions.q: Wrapper classes such as Integer and Double in Java are, like String, generally:
options: Mutable, so their wrapped value can be changed after creation
Immutable, meaning a new wrapper object is created rather than modifying the existing one's value

questions.q: Garbage collection in Java refers to:
options: Manual deletion of objects by the programmer using a delete keyword
The automatic process by which the JVM reclaims memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable/referenced
A compile-time process that removes unused classes
A method used to format source code

questions.q: Does Java provide a 'delete' keyword like C++ for manually freeing object memory?
options: Yes, Java has a delete keyword identical to C++
No, Java does not have a delete keyword; memory is reclaimed automatically by the garbage collector

questions.q: An object in Java becomes eligible for garbage collection when:
options: It is no longer reachable from any active part of the program (no live references point to it)
It is stored in a package

questions.q: Which method, if overridden in a class, was historically used to perform cleanup actions just before an object is garbage collected (though now discouraged/deprecated)?
Can a Java programmer force immediate garbage collection to occur at a specific moment?
options: Yes, calling System.gc() guarantees immediate collection
No, calling System.gc() only suggests/requests garbage collection to the JVM, but it does not guarantee immediate or even eventual execution
Yes, by using the delete keyword

questions.q: An array in Java is:
options: An object that holds a fixed-size, ordered collection of elements of the same type
A dynamically resizable collection similar to ArrayList by default

questions.q: How is the length of an array accessed in Java?
options: Using a method call like array.length()
Using the length field, e.g., array.length, without parentheses
Arrays do not have an accessible length in Java

questions.q: What is the default value of elements in a newly created int array in Java, if not explicitly initialized?
Once an array is created in Java with a fixed size, can that size be changed later?
options: Yes, arrays can be resized dynamically using a resize() method
No, the size of a Java array is fixed at creation time and cannot be changed; a new array must be created for a different size
Yes, but only for arrays of objects, not primitives
Only static arrays can be resized

questions.q: A two-dimensional array in Java, such as int[][] arr, can be thought of as:
options: A single row of elements only
An array of arrays, where each element is itself an array
A special primitive type distinct from int[]

questions.q: Which of the following correctly declares an array of integers in Java?
options: int arr[] = new int[5]; or int[] arr = new int[5];
